clinicalPearls: The classic triad is optic ataxia, simultanagnosia, and oculomotor apraxia
Optic ataxia is impaired visually guided reaching despite normal limb strength and proprioception
Simultanagnosia is the inability to perceive more than one object or the whole of a scene at a time despite seeing individual elements
Oculomotor apraxia (psychic gaze paralysis) is difficulty voluntarily directing the eyes to a target of interest
It results from bilateral parieto-occipital damage affecting the dorsal visual stream
Patients may appear functionally blind yet have intact primary visual fields on formal testing
Common causes include watershed infarction, posterior cortical atrophy, and other bilateral posterior lesions
reference.pathophysiology: Balint syndrome follows bilateral damage to the parieto-occipital junction, disrupting the dorsal visual stream that mediates spatial attention and visuomotor integration. Loss of this network produces simultanagnosia (a constricted attentional window), oculomotor apraxia (inability to voluntarily shift gaze), and optic ataxia (inaccurate visually guided reaching). Because primary visual cortex is relatively spared, elementary vision and fields can be preserved even though the patient behaves as if severely visually impaired. Typical causes are bilateral watershed infarction from hypotension, posterior cortical atrophy, and other diffuse or multifocal posterior pathology.
additionalDifferentials: Homonymous field defects from occipital lesions
Posterior cortical atrophy as an underlying cause
Apraxia and agnosia from other cortical lesions
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the brain focused on the bilateral parieto-occipital regions
Neuropsychological testing of visuospatial attention and visuomotor function
Formal visual field assessment to document preserved primary vision
Vascular imaging and evaluation for watershed infarction
Investigation for neurodegenerative disease when onset is insidious
Assessment for a precipitating hypotensive or hypoxic event
redFlags: Acute onset following hypotension or hypoxia suggesting watershed infarction
Progressive course suggesting posterior cortical atrophy or another degenerative process
Associated focal neurological signs indicating extensive posterior damage
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the cause; some recovery may occur after an isolated ischaemic or hypoxic insult with rehabilitation, whereas neurodegenerative causes progress, and the functional disability is often severe.
pitfalls: Mistaking the profound functional impairment for blindness despite intact visual fields
Attributing the picture to psychiatric or non-organic causes
Overlooking a treatable systemic precipitant of watershed ischaemia
Failing to recognise posterior cortical atrophy as an underlying degenerative cause
references: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
management: Treat the underlying cause, whether managing stroke risk factors and watershed infarction, correcting hypotension or hypoxia, or addressing an underlying neurodegenerative process
Provide multidisciplinary neurorehabilitation with occupational therapy targeting visuospatial attention, reaching and activities of daily living
Adapt the environment by decluttering, presenting single objects and using verbal and tactile cues to compensate for simultanagnosia and optic ataxia
Assess safety including fitness to drive and fall prevention, given the functional visual disability
Where posterior cortical atrophy or Alzheimer disease underlies the syndrome, involve neurology and consider cognitive-supportive pharmacotherapy
Refer for low-vision support and provide carer education and support
